title: Is it just a risk factor?
objectives: Regress pairs returns on factor returns.

screens.title: Pairs returns against the market
screens.prose: Each point is one six-month cycle: the market's return over its trading months, and the top 20's committed return. We take one cycle in six, so no two overlap. Turn the slope and watch the sum of squared residuals.

params.xLabel: Market return over the cycle's trading months

screens.question: Roughly which slope fits the cloud best?

options.text: Near 0
Near 1
options.why: A slope of 1 would mean the book moves with the market. Turn the slider to 1 and the squared residuals grow.

options.text: Near −1
options.why: A slope of −1 would make the book a short market position. The residuals grow there too.

feedback.correct: Correct. The best slope is close to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the slope until the sum of squared residuals is smallest.

explain.text: The least squares slope is 0.053: the cloud is close to flat. On average the book earns about the same whatever the market does. That slope is the book's **market beta**.

screens.title: The regression output
screens.prose: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) find pairs returns are not explained by standard risk factors. Our test regresses the 22 cycle returns on the market's return over the same months. The constant is the **alpha**.

state.caption: OLS of 22 cycle returns on the market, R² = 0.021.

screens.question: What is the alpha per month?

hints.text: The alpha is the constant's coefficient.
It is 0.0623 per six-month cycle.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the constant and divide by 6.

byKey.cycle: That is per six-month cycle. Divide by 6.
byKey.beta: That is the market coefficient, the beta.

explain.text: The alpha is 0.0623 a cycle, 1.04% a month, with t = 7.11. The beta is 0.0529 with t = 0.65. The market explains about 2% of the variation.

screens.title: Why the beta is small
screens.prose: Each pair is long £1 of one share and short £1 of another. In our panel every share carries the same market factor.

state.caption: OLS of 22 cycle returns on the market, R² = 0.021.

screens.question: Why is the book's beta close to 0?

options.text: The two legs carry the same market loading, so it cancels in each pair
The market rose over the twelve years
options.why: A rising market lifts both legs. Long one and short the other, the rise cancels.

options.text: Pairs trade rarely, so they hold no market risk
options.why: Our pairs are open most of the time. The legs cancel; idleness does not explain it.

options.text: The regression has only 22 points
options.why: Few points widen the error band. They do not pull the slope to 0.

hints.text: Write a pair's return as long leg minus short leg.
Each leg's market part is the same.
So the market part subtracts out.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what happens to the market part of long minus short.

explain.text: A pair's payoff is one leg's return minus the other's. With equal market loadings, the market moves both legs alike and cancels. What is left is the gap between the two, which is what the strategy trades.

screens.title: Reading the factor regression
screens.prose:
The regression splits each cycle's return into a part the market explains and a part it does not:
$$R_{p,c} = \alpha + \beta R_{m,c} + \varepsilon_c$$
A small $\beta$ says the market moves the book little. The $\alpha$ is the average return the market does not explain.
screens.question: With α = 0.0623 and β = 0.0529, what cycle return does the line predict when the market falls 10%?

hints.text: Put R_m = −0.10 into the line.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add alpha to beta times the market's return.

byKey.noalpha: You left out the alpha. The line starts at α.
byKey.sign: You added the market term. A fall of 10% enters as −0.10.

explain.text: 0.0623 + 0.0529 × (−0.10) = 0.0570, about 5.70% for the cycle. A 10% market fall costs the book about half a point. The prediction is an average; single cycles scatter widely around it.

screens.title: Which t to trust
screens.prose: On the 22 non-overlapping cycles the alpha's t is 7.11. On all 127 cycles, one starting each month, it is 13.48. Neighbouring cycles share five of their six months.

state.caption: OLS of 22 cycle returns on the market, R² = 0.021.

screens.question: Which figure should the note report?

options.text: 7.11, or a Newey-West t on all 127, because overlapping cycles are not independent
13.48, because more data gives a more accurate t
options.why: You counted overlapping cycles as new data. They repeat five months in six, so plain OLS overstates t.

options.text: Their average, to be fair to both
options.why: Averaging a sound and an inflated figure is still inflated.

options.text: Neither, because a t over 2 means nothing here
options.why: Either t is large. The question is which is honest.

hints.text: How many months do neighbouring cycles share?
Five of six.
Overlap inflates plain OLS t; use non-overlapping cycles or Newey-West.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Overlapping cycles are not independent observations.

explain.text: Plain OLS on overlapping cycles treats repeated months as new evidence, which inflates t from 7.11 to 13.48. Level 2 met the same problem with monthly figures. Replicating Momentum's "Standard errors for overlapping returns" gives the fix.

screens.title: Beta near zero, so riskless
screens.prose: A colleague reads β = 0.053 as proof the book is riskless. Yet with the wait 24 of 127 cycles lose money, the worst −10.8%. And the break cut the return by more than half.

params.xLabel: Market return over the cycle's trading months

screens.question: What does the small beta show?

options.text: Only that the market factor explains little; risks the market cannot see remain
That the book cannot lose money
options.why: You read zero beta as zero risk. 24 of 127 cycles lost money.

options.text: That the break must have been a market crash
options.why: The market barely moves the book. The break was in the pairs themselves.

options.text: That the alpha is luck
options.why: A t of 7.11 on 22 independent cycles is not luck. Beta says nothing about that.

hints.text: What risk did the break bring?
Pairs stopped co-moving; the market played no part.
Beta measures one risk, not all.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Beta measures exposure to one factor.

byKey.b: You read a beta near 0 as no risk at all. With the wait, 24 of 127 cycles lost money, the worst −10.8%.

explain.text: A beta near 0 rules out one risk: the market. The break, a pair-level risk, cut returns by more than half while the market regressor saw nothing. Losing cycles reach −10.8% with the wait.

screens.title: A common factor
screens.prose: The paper also finds that pairs returns share a common latent factor. We correlate the top 5's cycle returns with those of pairs 21 to 40. We do it before and after removing the market. Our panel plants no common factor.
screens.question: What does the result tell us?

options.text: No common factor here, as planted; it cannot test the paper's real-data finding
The paper was wrong about a common factor
options.why: Our panel was built without one. A test on it cannot overturn a finding on real data.

options.text: The two portfolios hedge each other
options.why: A correlation of −0.12 on 22 cycles is close to 0, well inside its noise.

options.text: Removing the market created a factor
options.why: The correlation barely moves, from −0.14 to −0.12.

hints.text: What did the generator plant?
Pair gaps are independent across pairs.
So the test can find no common factor here.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the generator planted.

explain.text: The residual correlation is −0.12 on 22 cycles and −0.07 on 127, near 0. That matches a panel with independent pair gaps. The seeded data can show the test works; only real data can test the paper's factor.

screens.title: An industry hedge that is not 1 to 1
screens.prose: Edge case. Two shares in one industry both load 1 on its factor. A cointegration hedge goes long £1 of A and short £0.60 of B, not £1.
screens.question: What net exposure to the industry factor does the position carry, in pounds?

hints.text: Long minus short, each times its loading.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract the short leg's exposure from the long leg's.

byKey.zero: That holds only for a 1 to 1 hedge. Here the legs differ.
byKey.sum: You added the legs. The short leg's exposure subtracts.

explain.text: With equal loadings, £1 long and £0.60 short leave £0.40 of the industry factor. Distance's 1 to 1 hedge cancels it; a cointegration hedge may not. Check industry exposure whenever the hedge ratio is far from 1.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
def pairs_panel(seed=2006, n_ind=10, per_ind=10, n_pairs=20, days=3024, half_life=8.0, ou_sd=0.008,
                rw_sd=0.015, break_day=1512, break_frac=0.8, half_spread=0.005):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N = n_ind * per_ind
    ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), per_ind)
    mkt = np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days))
    indf = np.cumsum(0.008 * rng.standard_normal((days, n_ind)), axis=0)
    phi = 0.5 ** (1.0 / half_life)
    u = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, N)), axis=0)        # unpaired: random walks
    common = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, n_pairs)), axis=0)
    eps = ou_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    a = np.zeros((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    for t in range(1, days):
        a[t] = phi * a[t - 1] + eps[t]                                   # mean-reverting gaps
    broken = rng.random(n_pairs) < break_frac
    drift = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs)), axis=0)
    for k in range(n_pairs):
        for j in (2 * k, 2 * k + 1):
            x = common[:, k] + a[:, j]
            if broken[k]:                                                # the pair stops co-moving
                x = x + np.where(np.arange(days) >= break_day, drift[:, j] - drift[break_day, j], 0.0)
            u[:, j] = x
    pair_ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), 2)[:n_pairs]
    ind[:2 * n_pairs] = np.repeat(pair_ind, 2)                           # two planted pairs an industry
    logp = np.log(50.0) + mkt[:, None] + indf[:, ind] + u
    mid = np.exp(logp)
    bounce = np.where(rng.random((days, N)) < 0.5, 1 + half_spread, 1 - half_spread)
    close = mid * bounce                                                 # closes at bid or ask
    return close, mid, ind, broken


def normalise(P):
    P = np.asarray(P, dtype=float)
    return P / P[0]


def ssd_matrix(Pn):
    G = Pn.T @ Pn
    d = np.diag(G)
    return d[:, None] + d[None, :] - 2 * G


def top_pairs(Pn, k):
    D = ssd_matrix(Pn)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(D.shape[0], 1)
    order = np.argsort(D[i, j], kind="stable")[:k]
    return [(int(i[o]), int(j[o])) for o in order]


def trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    sd = float(np.std(form[:, i] - form[:, j]))
    a, b = trade[:, i].tolist(), trade[:, j].tolist()
    n = len(a)
    payoff, opened, t = 0.0, False, 0
    while t < n:
        s = a[t] - b[t]
        if sd > 0 and abs(s) > open_at * sd and t + wait < n - 1:
            side = 1 if s > 0 else -1          # +1: i is dearer, so short i and buy j
            to = t + wait
            tc = next((u for u in range(t + 1, n) if (a[u] - b[u]) * side <= 0), None)
            tx = n - 1 if tc is None else min(tc + wait, n - 1)
            ri = (a[tx] - a[to]) / a[to]
            rj = (b[tx] - b[to]) / b[to]
            payoff += side * (rj - ri)
            opened = True
            t = tx + 1
            continue
        t += 1
    return payoff, opened


def trade_trips(form, trade, i, j, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    """Every round trip of trade_pair as (open day, close day, converged, payoff)."""
    sd = float(np.std(form[:, i] - form[:, j]))
    a, b = trade[:, i].tolist(), trade[:, j].tolist()
    n = len(a)
    trips, t = [], 0
    while t < n:
        s = a[t] - b[t]
        if sd > 0 and abs(s) > open_at * sd and t + wait < n - 1:
            side = 1 if s > 0 else -1
            to = t + wait
            tc = next((u for u in range(t + 1, n) if (a[u] - b[u]) * side <= 0), None)
            tx = n - 1 if tc is None else min(tc + wait, n - 1)
            pay = side * ((b[tx] - b[to]) / b[to] - (a[tx] - a[to]) / a[to])
            trips.append((to, tx, tc is not None, pay))
            t = tx + 1
            continue
        t += 1
    return trips


def cycle_return(close, start, k, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    """(committed, employed, opened) for the k closest pairs of the cycle from day start."""
    Pn = normalise(close[start:start + 378])
    form, trade = Pn[:252], Pn[252:]
    res = [trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait, open_at) for i, j in top_pairs(form, k)]
    total = sum(p for p, _ in res)
    n = sum(1 for _, o in res if o)
    return total / k, (total / n if n else 0.0), n


def run(close, k, wait=0, step=21, open_at=2.0):
    """[(start, committed return over the six trading months)] for every cycle."""
    return [(s, cycle_return(close, s, k, wait, open_at)[0]) for s in range(0, close.shape[0] - 378 + 1, step)]


def market_level(seed=2006, days=3024):
    """The panel's market index, exp(mkt), from the generator's first draw."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return np.exp(np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days)))

close, mid, ind, broken = pairs_panel()

M = market_level()

import numpy as np
def pairs_panel(seed=2006, n_ind=10, per_ind=10, n_pairs=20, days=3024, half_life=8.0, ou_sd=0.008,
                rw_sd=0.015, break_day=1512, break_frac=0.8, half_spread=0.005):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    N = n_ind * per_ind
    ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), per_ind)
    mkt = np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days))
    indf = np.cumsum(0.008 * rng.standard_normal((days, n_ind)), axis=0)
    phi = 0.5 ** (1.0 / half_life)
    u = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, N)), axis=0)        # unpaired: random walks
    common = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, n_pairs)), axis=0)
    eps = ou_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    a = np.zeros((days, 2 * n_pairs))
    for t in range(1, days):
        a[t] = phi * a[t - 1] + eps[t]                                   # mean-reverting gaps
    broken = rng.random(n_pairs) < break_frac
    drift = np.cumsum(rw_sd * rng.standard_normal((days, 2 * n_pairs)), axis=0)
    for k in range(n_pairs):
        for j in (2 * k, 2 * k + 1):
            x = common[:, k] + a[:, j]
            if broken[k]:                                                # the pair stops co-moving
                x = x + np.where(np.arange(days) >= break_day, drift[:, j] - drift[break_day, j], 0.0)
            u[:, j] = x
    pair_ind = np.repeat(np.arange(n_ind), 2)[:n_pairs]
    ind[:2 * n_pairs] = np.repeat(pair_ind, 2)                           # two planted pairs an industry
    logp = np.log(50.0) + mkt[:, None] + indf[:, ind] + u
    mid = np.exp(logp)
    bounce = np.where(rng.random((days, N)) < 0.5, 1 + half_spread, 1 - half_spread)
    close = mid * bounce                                                 # closes at bid or ask
    return close, mid, ind, broken


def normalise(P):
    P = np.asarray(P, dtype=float)
    return P / P[0]


def ssd_matrix(Pn):
    G = Pn.T @ Pn
    d = np.diag(G)
    return d[:, None] + d[None, :] - 2 * G


def top_pairs(Pn, k):
    D = ssd_matrix(Pn)
    i, j = np.triu_indices(D.shape[0], 1)
    order = np.argsort(D[i, j], kind="stable")[:k]
    return [(int(i[o]), int(j[o])) for o in order]


def trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    sd = float(np.std(form[:, i] - form[:, j]))
    a, b = trade[:, i].tolist(), trade[:, j].tolist()
    n = len(a)
    payoff, opened, t = 0.0, False, 0
    while t < n:
        s = a[t] - b[t]
        if sd > 0 and abs(s) > open_at * sd and t + wait < n - 1:
            side = 1 if s > 0 else -1          # +1: i is dearer, so short i and buy j
            to = t + wait
            tc = next((u for u in range(t + 1, n) if (a[u] - b[u]) * side <= 0), None)
            tx = n - 1 if tc is None else min(tc + wait, n - 1)
            ri = (a[tx] - a[to]) / a[to]
            rj = (b[tx] - b[to]) / b[to]
            payoff += side * (rj - ri)
            opened = True
            t = tx + 1
            continue
        t += 1
    return payoff, opened


def trade_trips(form, trade, i, j, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    """Every round trip of trade_pair as (open day, close day, converged, payoff)."""
    sd = float(np.std(form[:, i] - form[:, j]))
    a, b = trade[:, i].tolist(), trade[:, j].tolist()
    n = len(a)
    trips, t = [], 0
    while t < n:
        s = a[t] - b[t]
        if sd > 0 and abs(s) > open_at * sd and t + wait < n - 1:
            side = 1 if s > 0 else -1
            to = t + wait
            tc = next((u for u in range(t + 1, n) if (a[u] - b[u]) * side <= 0), None)
            tx = n - 1 if tc is None else min(tc + wait, n - 1)
            pay = side * ((b[tx] - b[to]) / b[to] - (a[tx] - a[to]) / a[to])
            trips.append((to, tx, tc is not None, pay))
            t = tx + 1
            continue
        t += 1
    return trips


def cycle_return(close, start, k, wait=0, open_at=2.0):
    """(committed, employed, opened) for the k closest pairs of the cycle from day start."""
    Pn = normalise(close[start:start + 378])
    form, trade = Pn[:252], Pn[252:]
    res = [trade_pair(form, trade, i, j, wait, open_at) for i, j in top_pairs(form, k)]
    total = sum(p for p, _ in res)
    n = sum(1 for _, o in res if o)
    return total / k, (total / n if n else 0.0), n


def run(close, k, wait=0, step=21, open_at=2.0):
    """[(start, committed return over the six trading months)] for every cycle."""
    return [(s, cycle_return(close, s, k, wait, open_at)[0]) for s in range(0, close.shape[0] - 378 + 1, step)]


def market_level(seed=2006, days=3024):
    """The panel's market index, exp(mkt), from the generator's first draw."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return np.exp(np.cumsum(0.0003 + 0.010 * rng.standard_normal(days)))

close, mid, ind, broken = pairs_panel()

M = market_level()
Y22 = [r for _, r in run(close, 20, 0, 126)]
Y22w = [r for _, r in run(close, 20, 1, 126)]
X22 = [M[s + 377] / M[s + 252] - 1 for s in range(0, 2647, 126)]

screens.title: The risk committee
screens.prose: A risk committee asks whether your pairs book is a disguised bet. One member suspects short volatility: steady gains, then a large loss when spreads blow out. Another suspects an industry bet.
screens.question: Which evidence answers both?

options.text: Regressions on market and industry factors, plus the worst cycles and what the pairs did in them
The market beta of 0.05 alone
options.why: Beta answers neither question. Short-volatility losses and industry tilts can both hide behind it.

options.text: The full-sample Sharpe ratio
options.why: A high Sharpe ratio is what a short-volatility book shows before its loss.

options.text: The number of pairs traded
options.why: A count says nothing about what the pairs are exposed to.

hints.text: Each suspicion names a factor or a pattern of losses.
Industry is a factor; short volatility shows in the worst cycles.
Test the factors and study the worst cycles.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each suspicion needs its own evidence.

explain.text: Industry regressions show whether the hedges leave a factor behind. The worst cycles show whether losses cluster when spreads widen and fail to converge. A small market beta settles neither.

ideas: On 22 non-overlapping cycles the top 20 earn α = 0.0623 a cycle (t 7.11) with β = 0.053 on the market.
The beta is small because each pair is long and short shares with the same market loading.
A small beta rules out market risk only. The break, a pair-level risk, cut returns by more than half.

formula.note: Use non-overlapping cycles or Newey-West errors.
